slides.title: Self-determination in outline
slides.text: A COLLECTIVE right — it belongs to a people, not to an individual — to decide autonomously on political status. Its ideological basis is the nineteenth-century nation-state idea, and its modern political impetus came from Wilson's Fourteen Points for a reordering of Europe. It entered the UN Charter as a purpose in Article 1(2) and Article 55, and was written as the common Article 1 of both 1966 Covenants — which is what turned it from a political principle into a treaty right.

terms.def: The collective right of a people to decide autonomously on its political status; Art 1(2) and 55 UN Charter, common Art 1 of the 1966 Covenants.

cards.q: Where is the right of self-determination positively anchored in international law?
cards.a: In Articles 1(2) and 55 of the UN Charter as a purpose of the Organization, and as the common Article 1 of both 1966 Covenants, which made it a treaty right.

slides.title: Who is a 'people'
slides.text: The weak point of the whole doctrine, because there is no agreed definition. The objective approach looks for commonalities of the group — ethnic origin, language, religion, culture, customs and traditions — PLUS a subjective belief in forming a common group. The alternative reading takes 'people' to mean the NATION, everyone living within the territorial boundaries of a state; this is the reading decolonization used, together with uti possidetis, under which the colonial administrative boundaries became the external frontiers. Which definition you adopt decides most self-determination cases before you reach the substance.

cards.q: What are the two competing definitions of a 'people' for self-determination, and what turns on the choice?
cards.a: The objective/subjective approach — shared ethnicity, language, religion, culture plus a belief in forming one group — and the territorial reading, the whole population of a state or colonial unit. The second, combined with uti possidetis, is what kept colonial boundaries intact and denies ethnic groups a separate claim.

slides.title: External and internal self-determination
slides.text: External self-determination is the right to establish one's own state, and it is the contested half. Secession is accepted in the colonial context; outside it, the most that is argued is REMEDIAL secession as an ultima ratio in cases of serious, systematic and widespread human rights violations — a claim the ICJ pointedly did not resolve in the Kosovo advisory opinion. Internal self-determination is the safer half: free choice of one's own status and of the political, economic, social and cultural order, without outside interference — which is why the slide links it to the prohibition of intervention. Whether it extends to a right of political participation or to autonomy for ethnic minorities is open.

terms.def: The contested claim that a people subjected to grave and systematic human rights violations may secede as a last resort.

cards.q: Does self-determination give an ethnic minority within a state the right to secede?
cards.a: As a rule no. External self-determination in the sense of a right to statehood is confined to the colonial context; outside it only remedial secession is argued, as an ultima ratio against serious, systematic and widespread human rights violations — and the ICJ left the question open in the Kosovo opinion. Internal self-determination is what such a group can claim.

External: the right to establish one's own state — confined to decolonization, with remedial secession contested. Internal: free choice of political status and of the political, economic, social and cultural order without outside interference.

slides.title: The idea of human rights
slides.text: Rights of the individual against their OWN state: defensive rights such as freedom of opinion and expression, which the state may not interfere with and must guarantee. They developed in domestic law — Great Britain, France, the United States — and until the early twentieth century how a state treated its own nationals was regarded as a purely domestic matter within its sovereign regulatory powers. Minority protection after the First World War was the first breach; the comprehensive approach came after the Second, in Articles 55(c) and 56 of the Charter.

cards.q: What changed after 1945 in the international law view of how a state treats its own nationals?
cards.a: Until then it was a purely domestic matter within sovereign regulatory powers, breached only by interwar minority protection. Articles 55(c) and 56 of the Charter made respect for human rights a matter of international concern and obligation.

slides.title: Human rights versus diplomatic protection
slides.text: The clearest way to see what human rights changed. Diplomatic protection is a right OF THE STATE to have its own nationals protected abroad — the law on the treatment of foreigners — and nationality is decisive. Human rights are rights OF THE INDIVIDUAL against their own state; nationality is irrelevant and the individual is the holder. Two consequences follow: the individual is no longer 'mediatized' by their own state, and they can enforce the rights themselves — through quasi-judicial procedures in the UN system and individual complaints before regional courts. The slide adds one more pairing: human rights apply in peacetime and in armed conflict, humanitarian law only in conflict.

terms.def: The older position in which an individual could reach international law only through their own state; human rights ended it.

cards.q: How do human rights differ from diplomatic protection in who holds the right?
cards.a: Diplomatic protection is the STATE's right, exercised on behalf of its nationals abroad, and nationality is decisive. Human rights belong to the INDIVIDUAL against their own state, nationality is irrelevant, and the individual can enforce them personally.

cards.q: Do human rights apply during armed conflict?
cards.a: Yes — human rights apply in peacetime and in armed conflict; humanitarian law applies only in conflict. The two regimes overlap rather than exclude each other.

slides.title: Sources I: the Declaration and the Covenants
slides.text: The Universal Declaration of 1948 is a General Assembly resolution and per se not legally binding — with two arguments for binding force anyway: that it has become customary law, and that it is an authentic interpretation of the Charter. Then the 1966 Covenants. The Covenant on Civil and Political Rights carries the classic defensive rights: life, prohibition of torture and slavery, liberty of the person, private life, religion, fair trial and due process, and political rights of expression, assembly and demonstration. The Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights carries rights to work, education, social security and health care, and cultural services.

terms.def: The two 1966 Covenants: civil and political rights, and economic, social and cultural rights.

cards.q: The UDHR is not binding as such. On what two arguments is it nevertheless treated as law?
cards.a: That its content has passed into customary international law, and that it constitutes an authentic interpretation of the human rights provisions of the UN Charter.

slides.title: Sources II: specific and regional treaties
slides.text: The specific UN conventions: Genocide 1948, Racial Discrimination 1965, Discrimination against Women 1979, Torture 1984, Children's Rights 1989, Persons with Disabilities 2006. The regional conventions: the European Convention on Human Rights 1950, the American Convention 1969, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights 1981. And the Council of Europe's specialised instruments: the European Social Charter 1961, the Charter of Regional and Minority Languages 1992, the Framework Convention on National Minorities 1995 and the Istanbul Convention on domestic violence 2011.

cards.q: Name the three regional human rights conventions and their years.
cards.a: The European Convention on Human Rights 1950, the American Convention on Human Rights 1969 and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights 1981.

slides.title: When rights may be restricted
slides.text: Very few rights are absolute — the prohibitions of torture, slavery and apartheid. Everything else may be limited, and a lawful limitation has three requirements which you should apply in order. It must have a basis in a specific LAW setting out the conditions of its application. It must be NECESSARY for a legitimate purpose — a public interest such as national security, territorial integrity, public order and crime prevention, or health or morals; or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others, such as reputation or confidentiality. And it must be PROPORTIONATE: is the restriction appropriate to attain the desired result, and is it the least interfering means of reaching it?

cards.q: Set out the three-step test for a lawful restriction of a human right.
cards.a: A basis in a specific law setting out the conditions; necessity for a legitimate purpose (public interest or the rights of others); and proportionality — appropriate to the aim and the least interfering means available.

cards.q: Which human rights admit of no restriction at all?
cards.a: The prohibitions of torture, of slavery and of apartheid/racial discrimination — the few absolute rights.

slides.title: Enforcement: judicial, quasi-judicial, political
slides.text: Three levels, in descending order of teeth. JUDICIAL enforcement exists only regionally: the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, the Inter-American Court in San José and the African Court in Arusha, hearing individual and inter-state complaints — with the International Criminal Court a separate and differently-shaped body. QUASI-JUDICIAL enforcement runs through treaty bodies such as the Human Rights Committee under the ICCPR, again on individual or state complaints. POLITICAL enforcement is unilateral by states or multilateral: reporting by states and by UN bodies, Special Rapporteurs on torture or disappearances, the Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, and ultimately the Security Council. Note the gap the list exposes — there is no universal human rights COURT.

terms.def: A committee of experts monitoring a human rights treaty; its views on individual complaints are authoritative but not binding judgments.

cards.q: Where can an individual bring a binding judicial human rights claim, and where not?
cards.a: Only at the regional level — the European, Inter-American and African human rights courts. At the universal level there is no human rights court, only quasi-judicial treaty bodies such as the Human Rights Committee, whose views do not bind.
